Re: Public Records Act Request

Dear Alpine Community Planning Group Members,

Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, I am writing to request a copy of the records detailed below.

I am researching how the Alpine Community Planning Group (ACPG) conducts its business on the part of the residents of Alpine in preparation for publication of an expose. To that end, I request the following records:

1. All Alpine Community Planning Group Agendas and Minutes from 1 January 2024 through 31 May 2025.

2. All communications between any member of the Alpine Community Planning Group and another member(s) of the Alpine Community Planning Group from 1 January 2024 through 31 May 2025. Please include current and former members during this time period.

3. All communications between any member of the Alpine Community Planning Group and another government agency, including between the group members and the County of San Diego from 1 January 2024 through 31 May 2025. Please include current and former members during this time period.

4. All communications between any member of the Alpine Community Planning Group and any member of the public, including between the group members and individuals/entities with business before the group from 1 January 2024 through 31 May 2025. Please include current and former members during this time period.

Please note that the Public Records Act allows a member of the public to request records by describing their content, rather than asking for specific documents by name; an agency that receives such a request must “search for records based on criteria set forth in the search request.”

Public records represent “any handwriting, typewriting, printing, photostating, photographing, photocopying, transmitting by electronic mail or facsimile, and every other means of recording upon any tangible thing any form of communication or representation, including letters, words, pictures, sounds, or symbols, or combinations thereof, and any record thereby created, regardless of the manner in which the record has been stored.” (Government Code section 7920.545.)

1. This request applies to all records in your agency’s possession, including documents created by a member of another government agency or a member of the public.

2. If specific portions of any documents are exempt from disclosure, please provide the non-exempt portions.

3. Please provide entire documents, even if only parts of them are responsive to this request.

If you maintain records or data in electronic format, please provide them in that same format.

1 California First Amendment Coalition v. Superior Court, 67 Cal.App.4th 159, 165-66 (1998).
2 See California State University v. Superior Court, 90 Cal. App. 4th 810, 824-25 (1999).
3 Gov’t. Code § 6253(a). versions are acceptable) to avoid copying costs.
4 If you are unable to reproduce electronic records in electronic form, please provide a reason for doing so.

I request that you waive copying fees because I have limited resources, and the information requested will be used in the public interest to further the public’s understanding of the local community planning group action. None of the information obtained will be sold or distributed for profit. If you are unable to waive the copying fees, and you anticipate that these costs will exceed $50, or that the time needed to copy the records will delay their release, please contact me so that we can arrange to inspect the document or decide which documents we wish to have copied. Otherwise, please copy and send them as soon as possible. Please respond to this request within ten (10) days, either by providing all the requested records or by providing a written response setting forth the legal authority for withholding or redacting any document and stating when the documents will be made available.

If you require any clarification in identifying responsive documents or focusing this request, please contact [redacted]. Please send all records responsive to this request to Louis Russo.

Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

[redacted]

Gov’t. Code § 6253.9.
Gov’t. Code §§ 6253(c), 6255.
Gov’t. Code § 6253.1.

	(2) Recommended participants (external stakeholders, other agencies)?

	I think the two questions are somewhat related in that the capacity of the location would determine how many people are invited. And to consider the County’s own buildings as part of this effort, we may need to include the Department of General Services and/or other departments. 	Hi Murtaza,

	Here is what we have so far:

	The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

	Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

	Let us know what you think.

Subject: RWER Data Collection Support: Data for County-owned Land

Hi Krista,

I hope you’re doing well!  I’m working with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) to develop the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER); our team is collecting data to support development of the report. We recently had a meeting with Fali Field, as well, to request GIS location data on County-owned facilities  (not leased). We’ll be receiving an excel data table with locations of owned facilities & CPNs, and she recommend I reach out to you to see if we could receive similar location and CPN data for county owned land. The purpose of this data collection is to identify sites that may be good candidates for stormwater capture, storage and reuse, and diversion projects.

Would you be able to provide the data for our currently owned land parcels? Ideally, we’d like to receive this data by the end of this week (June 2nd); would that be possible? I’m also happy to meet with you and provide more context on the project, and have included a bit of background on the report we’re developing the reason for the request.

Background

In September 2022, our Board directed staff to analyze drought management and water sustainability practices and to address our region’s reliance on water resources. The effort is binational and regional in scale and includes a comprehensive regional assessment of San Diego County, as well as interviews with Imperial County and water agencies in Tijuana to identify recommendations (projects) to support addressing the drought equitably. Proposed recommendations are to be aligned with California’s Water Supply Strategy, which includes creating new storage for water to capitalize on big storms, recycle/reuse water to enable safter use of wastewater that we currently discharge to the ocean, improve efficient water use and conservation and creating “new water” through stormwater capture/reuse, desalination, and diversification of supplies.

The OSEJ is leading this multi-county/binational effort, and DPW WPP is helping to collect data, among other tasks. We’re currently at the end of our data collection process and conducting stakeholder interviews with support of our consulting team. Data collection examples include identifying opportunities on county-owned land/facilities where stormwater capture/use and storage can be implemented, as well as opportunities for water diversion.

Best,

emails.subject: Bob Figari 5th annual LA to SF ride for the Arthritis Foundation in September 2024
emails.body:
Hello, my dear friends and family!

I’m bicycling again for the fifth year starting September 21 from San Francisco to Los Angeles for the Arthritis Foundation. I am so grateful to all of you who have donated in the past for this event. It’s hard for me to ask you again for money, but this is the way I can help the most. And it is an easy way for you to participate without getting your rear sore! Please pardon the form letter. Often, I hear directly from some of you. I love that as it gives us both a chance to catch up in a more personal way.

For the past three years you have made me a top California Coastal Classic (CCC) fundraiser. The money we raise benefits many of us Boomers, but most importantly it helps the kids and young adults who suffer from arthritis. The CCC has been such a successful fundraising event that the Arthritis Foundation is copying our ride blueprint for similar events throughout the nation. Pretty cool that all of us are associated with such a dynamic, successful and influential philanthropic organization.

A very special thanks to Joel, Danny, Kris and Chris I, who have been incredibly generous in past donations. And to so many of you who have consistently donated for five years, I’m so grateful. You’re awesome!

The Pitch. . .  . ⚾️
Please support me with a tax-deductible donation to the Arthritis Foundation (a 501 (c) (3) charity). I’m donating $3500 from my IRA toward a fundraising goal of $15,000 and I’m hoping you will help me reach that goal.

To make your donation and get information about the ride, use this link to my CCC page:

https://events.arthritis.org/index.cfm?fuseaction=donordrive.participant&participantID=333448   Click on “Support Me” and follow the instructions.

[Special note for those of you who have IRAs that involve a Required Minimum Distribution (RMD):
You can make a charitable donation directly from your IRA to help satisfy the RMD. The donation check must come directly from your IRA and be made out to the Arthritis Foundation. I’ve attached the form to use for sending the check to the Arthritis Foundation. If you make a IRA check donation you have to use this form so that I and my team get credit.]

Trip Details       🚴🏻
For those interested in trip details, we cycle 8 days from September 21 to 28 along country roads and highways 525 miles over 8 days from San Francisco to Los Angeles. We average about 68 miles per day. We’ll travel through Santa Cruz, Monterey and Carmel, Big Sur, Cambria, Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Foxen Canyon, Los Olivos, Santa Barbara, Ventura and Malibu, ending at Pepperdine University. All but one slide has been repaired along Highway 1, so hopefully we can ride directly from Big Sur to Cambria. If not, we have an alternative route from Los Robles to Cambria in the works.

CCC riders can camp out at specially reserved campsites or stay in hotels along the way. I’m camping again this year except for one lodge stay in Cambria which about half way. I like the fellowship and proximity to the beer and BBQ that the camping option offers! But, I do look forward to a real bed and shower in Cambria!

We are very well fed every morning and evening. SAG wagons follow us in case of either bike breakdowns or body breakdowns. So far, I haven’t had to make use of either. And we have rest stops along the way that are supported by volunteers who create an amazing spread of PBJs, dill pickles, energy drinks and supplements provided by our sponsors, and other delectable delights. Oh, and don’t forget the availability of restrooms!

The toughest day for me is the Day 1 SF to Santa Cruz ride of 88 miles. My legs do okay, but my rear end doesn’t like going past about 60 miles! Don’t feel to sorry for me though . . . we can purchase a 50 minute session at our traveling massage tent. I’m probably their best customer the entire week.

My favorite end of day spot is the Big Sur River Inn. The restaurant there provides fabulous food which you can eat while sitting in Adirondack chairs that have been placed right in the middle of the stream. The sensation of putting tired feet into the cooling waters while munching on a hamburger and drinking a beer is sublime.

Most of the trip is safe from serious traffic, but going through Malibu area on the last day feels like a gauntlet.  There is no bike lane, so we ride in-between the cars parked along the shoulders and weekend traffic racing down the winding coastal road. I wear my brightest cycling outfit and make sure my flashing lights are fully charged!

Family News  🧑‍🧑‍🧒‍🧒🇺🇸🇭🇷
On the family side of things, my wife, Chris and I had a fabulous trip to Helsinki, Norway and Amsterdam in March. Most of our time was spent on a small boat cruise through the Arctic waters north of Tromso, Norway and a Malangen lodge stay on a Norwegian bay. On the cruise we did actual dogsledding with me steering and braking while Chris was hanging on for dear life. We also rafted into hidden fjords, saw leaping sperm whales, hung out with reindeer, did two arctic plunges into the 1 deg C sea and were amazed by the Northern Lights. At Malangen, we did cross country skiing, drank incredible Norwegian gin, ate reindeer and even whale, and topped it off with hot tubbing and saunaing in a blizzard along the lakeshore. Helsinki and Amsterdam were also fabulous including ferrying through the ice filled bays of Helsinki to historic sites and dining with a couple friends at night in a tiny boat along the canals of Amsterdam. Highly recommend it all!

In April/May, we had visitors for a month from Croatia . . . the parents of our son’s husband. All six of us traveled together for two weeks for 4000 miles in my pickup truck to the Grand Canyon, Bryce, Zion, Las Vegas, Sequoia, Yosemite, Marin County and down the coast to Santa Barbara and then home. Wow! We loved every second of the trip, even riding together! We stayed in AirBnBs along the way.The sights were amazing. A standout for me was Yosemite. I climbed Half Dome a couple

Subject: UCSD workshops

Dear UCSD team,

The approach on the following workshops has been approved. The next steps for the UCSD team are:

Workshop #1: Please place a hold on November 7 on all your calendars and reserve the PEB space. It would be helpful to begin drafting an agenda/program that we would be discuss with Sarah on September 2.
Workshop #2: We will be coordinating with the Planning and Development Services Department and get back to you.
Workshop #3: It would be helpful if we can develop a timeline. We will be coordinating with our Vice Chair Nora Vargas.

Thank you!
Murtaza
____________________________

  1.  Enterprise-wide Alignment of RDF
Date: November 7, 2022 (back-up would be November 4, 2022)
Participants:  County of San Diego internal department leadership, internal stakeholders
Duration: Full-day 2-part workshop
Location: 7th floor terrace at the Public Engagement Building

This workshop would provide an initial convening of County of San Diego leadership and departments engaged in the implementation of decarbonization across municipal functions:  (1) Departmental Sustainability Planning, led by LUEG; (2) the Land Acquisition Roundtable, led by Parks & Recreation; and (3) the renewable energy siting framework in the RDF.  This workshop would focus on the County departments’ short/mid/long term goals towards sustainability; geospatial and policy relationships, conflicts, and potential synergies among and between land acquisition for park, conservation, and recreation purposes; and the extent of land area for new solar and wind energy required by alternative strategies in the RDF.  This approach would help build a common understanding of the policy levers and constraints for the departments in relationship to GHG reduction, and the distribution and extent of each set of land use needs, supporting the goal of identifying potential synergies including opportunities for multi-benefit uses of land for agriculture, water and watershed sustainability, recreation, and regional habitat linkage.

***This workshop would be in tandem with the preparation of document defining the scope of work regarding the team’s advisory role for LUEG and the RDF. [Ref: Tasks 2.1 & 2.2]

  2.  Sustainable Land Use Framework (SLUF)
Timeline: Early 2023
Participants: County’s Planning & Development Services Department, external stakeholders
Location: First floor lab on the ground floor of the Public Engagement Building

This workshop will focus on the themes adopted by the Board in September 2022 in the context of the General Plan for the unincorporated area of the County. It would not be framed as RDF implementation but would examine the potential alignments of SLUF with decarbonization pathways. These themes could include: (1) decarbonization of buildings, communities, and transportation through policies and land use; (2) increase opportunities for sustainable and resilient development and housing for all; (3) support green economies, innovative infrastructure, agriculture, and sustainable best practices; (4) conserve and protect existing natural habitats and resources, and increase access to open and green spaces; and (5) prioritize social equity and environmental justice in sustainable land use policies, programs, and plans.

  3.  Binational Regional Climate Action Plan
Timeframe:  Last quarter 2023/first quarter 2024
Participants:  Jurisdictions in San Diego County with CAPs (municipalities; SANDAG; Unified Port of San Diego; US Department of Defense); California Office of Policy & Research
Invited Guests:  Governments of Baja California Norte; City of Tijuana; UABC

The third workshop would engage stakeholders across the county and San Diego-Tijuana region in evaluating the consistency and commonality of purpose and strategies among and between the individual Climate Action Plans (CAPs) adopted pursuant to State directives and local initiative.  UCSD students would prepare assessments of each plan in a unified framework illustrating the baselines, policies, action steps, and reporting metrics across the region.  The workshop will focus on building common awareness and purpose; exchanging strategies and ideas; identifying areas of potential re-alignment; and building a binational baseline for emissions and measures. This workshop would explore the possibility of a Binational Regional Climate Action Plan.
